```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(idiographic)
data(srl)
```

Intensive longitudinal data record the same persons on many occasions, and
the questions they address concern processes within persons, such as whether
the state of a person on one occasion relates to other states of that person
on the same or the following occasion. Raw scores are an imperfect basis for
these questions. Each raw score combines the stable level at which a person
typically stands with the deviation of the occasion from that level, so an
association computed on raw scores mixes a between-person association with a
within-person association. The two associations answer different questions
and can differ in size and in sign [@curran2011; @hoffman2009]. A raw score
also holds no information about earlier occasions, while any claim about
temporal precedence requires the state on one occasion to be paired with a
later state of the same person. Scores that change systematically over the
study period, through learning, fatigue or habituation, share that change
across variables, and a shared trend produces an association between two
variables whose occasion-to-occasion fluctuations are independent.

Panel preparation removes these sources of bias before modelling. The
decomposition of a variable separates its between-person and within-person
components, a lagged variable pairs each occasion with the preceding occasion of
the same person, and detrending removes a linear change over the study
period. Each transformation is computed separately for each person and in
time order.

```{r data-values, include = FALSE}
n_learners <- length(unique(srl$name))
n_days <- length(unique(srl$day))
n_obs <- format(nrow(srl), big.mark = ",")
```

The examples use the `r n_learners` learners in `srl`, each observed on
`r n_days` days.

## Within-person and between-person decomposition

A variable measured repeatedly varies between persons and within persons. A
learner can report high efficacy on most days because high efficacy is a
stable characteristic of that learner, and the same learner reports higher
efficacy on some days than on others. The two sources of variation correspond
to different mechanisms. The between-person association concerns stable
differences, whether learners who are generally more efficacious also
generally invest more effort. The within-person association concerns a
process, whether a learner invests more effort on days when that learner
feels more efficacious than usual. The first characterises a population of
persons and the second characterises the functioning of each person, and the
inference from one to the other holds only under restrictive conditions
[@molenaar2004].

A regression of raw scores estimates a weighted combination of the two
slopes, with weights given by the share of the predictor's variance at each
level [@curran2011]. When the two slopes differ, the pooled slope matches
neither, and its value depends on the composition of the sample. Entering the
person mean and the deviation from it as separate predictors resolves this
conflation [@mundlak1978; @hoffman2009]. The deviation is uncorrelated with
the person mean by construction. Its slope is therefore a within-person
estimate that is unaffected by any stable characteristic of the person,
whether measured or unmeasured, which is the property of the fixed-effects
estimator.

For a variable $x$ observed for person $i$ at occasion $t$, the
between-person component is the person mean, the mean of that person's
observed values,
$$\bar{x}_i = \frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t=1}^{T_i} x_{it},$$
where $T_i$ is the number of occasions on which $x$ was observed. The
within-person component is the person-mean-centred score
$x_{it} - \bar{x}_i$, the deviation of each occasion from the person mean,
and the two components sum to the original score. `split_levels()` adds both
components to the data as variables, for efficacy as `efficacy_between` and
`efficacy_within`.

```{r decompose}
split_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = "efficacy", time = "day", keep_all = FALSE) |> head()
```

```{r split-values, include = FALSE}
# fit_within_between() holds out the last ceiling(test_prop * n) occasions of
# each person, with test_prop = 0.2 by default.
test_days <- ceiling(0.2 * n_days)
train_days <- n_days - test_days
n_train <- format(n_learners * train_days, big.mark = ",")
```

The between-person component `efficacy_between` and the within-person
component `efficacy_within` enter the same regression as predictors of
effort. The slope of `efficacy_within` is the within-person effect, the
change in effort on days when a learner's efficacy deviates from that
learner's mean. The slope of `efficacy_between` is the between-person effect,
the difference in mean effort between learners whose mean efficacy differs.
`fit_within_between()` estimates the regression on the first `r train_days`
days of each learner and holds out the last `r test_days` days to evaluate
its predictions, and the person means are computed from the estimation days
only. The `r n_train` estimation days are nested in `r n_learners` learners,
and observations of the same learner are correlated. Standard errors that
treat the observations as independent understate the uncertainty, so the
standard errors are clustered on the learner [@liang1986].

```{r within-between}
wb_fit <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort", x = "efficacy", id = "name", time = "day")
coefs(wb_fit)
```

```{r within-between-values, include = FALSE}
wb_terms <- subset(coefs(wb_fit), term != "(Intercept)")
within_row <- subset(wb_terms, component == "within")
between_row <- subset(wb_terms, component == "between")
two_dp <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
ten_points <- \(slope) sprintf("%.0f", 10 * slope)
```

The within-person slope is `r two_dp(within_row$estimate)` (95% CI
`r two_dp(within_row$conf_low)` to `r two_dp(within_row$conf_high)`). On
days when a learner's efficacy is 10 points above that learner's mean, effort
is about `r ten_points(within_row$estimate)` points higher. The
between-person slope is `r two_dp(between_row$estimate)` (95% CI
`r two_dp(between_row$conf_low)` to `r two_dp(between_row$conf_high)`).
Learners whose mean efficacy is 10 points higher report about
`r ten_points(between_row$estimate)` points more effort on average. The
between-person interval is wider because its precision depends on the number
of learners, `r n_learners`, while the within-person slope draws on the daily
deviations of all learners.

The difference between the between-person and the within-person slope is the
contextual effect [@mundlak1978]. It measures the association of the person
mean with the outcome beyond the association implied by the within-person
slope. A positive contextual effect indicates that learners with higher mean
efficacy invest more effort than their daily relation between efficacy and
effort predicts, which is consistent with stable characteristics, such as
motivation or prior achievement, that raise both mean efficacy and mean
effort.

```{r contextual}
contextual(wb_fit)
```

```{r contextual-values, include = FALSE}
context_row <- as.data.frame(contextual(wb_fit))
p_text <- sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", context_row$p_value))
```

The between-person slope exceeds the within-person slope by
`r two_dp(context_row$contextual)` (95% CI
`r sprintf("%.3f", context_row$conf_low)` to `r two_dp(context_row$conf_high)`,
p = `r p_text`). The lower bound of the interval lies close to zero, and the
evidence for a difference between the two slopes is weak.

## Lagged variables

Many hypotheses about within-person processes concern effects that unfold
over time, such as whether the efficacy of a learner on one day predicts the
effort of that learner on the following day. A test of such a hypothesis
requires a predictor measured before the outcome. Temporal precedence is also
a necessary condition for a causal interpretation. Two variables measured at
the same time can each be the cause of the other, whereas a variable measured
earlier can only act on a later outcome. A lagged variable establishes this
order by pairing each observation with the preceding observation of the same
person. With `lag = 1`, the column `efficacy_lag1` holds, in each row, the
efficacy of the learner on the preceding day.

The pairing yields two kinds of lagged effect. The autoregressive effect, the
slope of a variable on its own lagged value, measures the persistence of a
state from one occasion to the next, often termed inertia. The cross-lagged
effect, the slope of one variable on the lagged value of another, measures
whether a deviation in one state precedes a deviation in the other, for
example whether efficacy above a learner's mean on one day predicts effort
above the mean on the next day. These two effects are the parameters of the
vector autoregressive models that underlie dynamic networks
[@bringmann2013; @epskamp2018mlvar]. Precedence is a necessary condition and
remains insufficient on its own, since a third variable that changes before
both can produce a cross-lagged association.

Lags are computed within persons, so each lagged value comes from the same
person as the row it occupies. The first observation of each person has no
preceding observation and receives a missing lagged value, as the first days
of Aisha show.

```{r lags}
lagged <- preprocess_panel(srl, id = "name", time = "day", vars = "efficacy", lag = 1, keep_all = FALSE)
head(lagged)
```

```{r lag-values, include = FALSE}
n_lag_missing <- sum(is.na(lagged$efficacy_lag1))
n_after_gap <- n_lag_missing - n_learners
```

Of the `r n_obs` lagged values, `r n_lag_missing` are missing,
`r n_learners` for the first days of the learners and `r n_after_gap` for
days that follow a day without an efficacy rating.

The size of a lagged effect depends on the interval between occasions. An
effect that unfolds within hours appears stronger over a lag of one hour than
over a lag of one day, and lagged effects are therefore comparable only
between designs with similar intervals [@gollob1987]. A lag refers to the
preceding occasion whatever the elapsed time, which is appropriate when
occasions are evenly spaced, as the consecutive days in `srl` are for every
learner. In designs with irregular spacing, such as experience sampling at
random times or diaries with skipped days, `lag_max_gap` sets the lagged
value to missing when the preceding occasion lies further back than a
specified interval, so that a lag spanning several days stays out of a model
of day-to-day effects.

## Detrending

The within-person models of the later vignettes assume that each series is
stationary, with a mean and a variance that stay constant over the study
period. A series that rises or falls systematically violates this
assumption. Its deviations from the person mean are then dominated by the
trend, negative early in the study and positive late in the study, and an
autoregressive model attributes the resulting dependence between
neighbouring occasions to the persistence of the state. When two variables
share a trend, their deviations correlate across occasions whatever their
day-to-day relation, a spurious association well documented for time series
[@granger1974]. Detrending regresses the series of each person on time and
retains the residuals, so that the within-person component expresses the
fluctuation around the trajectory of the person [@wang2015].

Removing a trend is a substantive decision. A trend can be a nuisance, such
as a gradual habituation to the questionnaire, or the phenomenon of
interest, such as a growth in efficacy over a course. In the second case
detrending removes the effect under study, and time belongs in the model as
a predictor.

`preprocess_panel(detrend = "person")` fits a linear trend to the series of
each person and removes it when the slope is significant at `detrend_alpha`,
0.05 by default. The presence of trends is assessed beforehand with the trend
tests that `describe_persons()` reports for each person and variable.

```{r trends}
trends <- describe_persons(srl, id = "name", time = "day", vars = "efficacy:organizing", detail = "full")
summary(trends)
```

```{r trend-values, include = FALSE}
trend_summary <- summary(trends)
n_trending <- sum(trend_summary$significant_trends)
n_series <- sum(trend_summary$persons)
n_variables <- nrow(trend_summary)
trend_pct <- sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * n_trending / n_series)
n_expected <- sprintf("%.0f", 0.05 * n_series)
number_word <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")
```

Across the `r number_word[n_variables]` variables, `r n_trending` of the
`r n_series` person-by-variable series (`r trend_pct`) have a significant
linear trend. With `r n_series` tests at the 0.05 level and no trend in any
series, about `r n_expected` significant results are expected by chance. The
observed count therefore gives no evidence of systematic trends, and
detrending these data would alter a small number of series largely at
random. Detrending is warranted when significant trends are considerably
more frequent than the significance level, or when the design implies a
trend, as in intervention or developmental studies.

A linear detrend suits a deterministic trend, a steady change in the mean. A
stochastic trend, as in a random walk, wanders without a fixed slope and is
removed by differencing, the replacement of each value by its change from
the preceding occasion. `preprocess(detrend = "auto")` tests each series for
both kinds of trend and applies linear detrending or differencing to the
flagged series only.

## Centring and scaling

Centring subtracts a mean from each score. The mean that is subtracted
decides whether the differences between persons remain in the scores, and
therefore whether a slope estimated on the centred scores is a within-person
effect. Person-centring (`center = "person"`) subtracts the person mean from
each score and retains only the within-person component. It is the
appropriate transformation when the research question concerns within-person
processes alone, as in dynamic network models. In a multilevel
autoregressive model, lagged predictors left uncentred carry the
between-person differences in level, and the autoregressive effect then
mixes the persistence of daily states with the stable differences between
persons [@hamaker2015]. Grand-mean centring (`center = "grand"`) subtracts
one mean computed over all persons and occasions. It gives the intercept the
interpretation of the expected outcome at the sample mean and leaves the
between-person differences in the scores, so a slope on grand-mean-centred
scores remains the combination of the within-person and the between-person
slope [@enders2007]. Person-centring and decomposition are alternatives,
because person-centring discards the between-person component that
decomposition retains, and `preprocess_panel()` refuses a request for both.

```{r scale-values, include = FALSE}
person_sd <- aggregate(efficacy ~ name, data = srl, FUN = sd)
sd_range <- sprintf("%.1f", range(person_sd$efficacy))
```

Scaling sets the unit of a variable. Person scaling (`scale = "person"`)
divides the scores of each person by that person's standard deviation.
Slopes then express change in standard deviations of the person, which makes
them comparable across persons who fluctuate to different degrees. In
`srl`, the within-person standard deviation of efficacy ranges from
`r sd_range[1]` to `r sd_range[2]` points across learners. Person scaling
also removes these differences in variability, and within-person variability
is itself an individual difference with substantive meaning, such as
emotional instability. A slope on person-scaled scores combines the strength
of an association with the variability of the predictor and reports the two
as one quantity. Grand scaling (`scale = "grand"`) divides all scores by one
standard deviation, which changes the unit of measurement and preserves the
differences in variability between persons.

`preprocess_panel()` and `split_levels()` compute person means, standard
deviations and trends from all occasions of each person. When a model is
evaluated on held-out occasions, quantities computed from all occasions
carry information from the held-out occasions into the estimation and
inflate the measured predictive accuracy. `fit_within_between()` therefore
computes the person means from the estimation occasions only and applies
them to the held-out occasions, and the transformations of
`preprocess_panel()` are suited to descriptive analyses and to models
estimated without held-out occasions.
